ἀθροίζουσι γὰρ οὗτοι τάχιστα πλῆθος, ἐλλιπῶς διαπνεόμε- νοι καὶ διὰ τοῦτο τῆς ἀναδόσεως ἰσχομένης αὐτοῖς, ὑγρὰ μὲν πάντως γίνεται τὰ διαχωρήματα, ποτὲ δ᾿ οὐχ ὑγρὰ μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ λεπτὰ καὶ μάλιστα ἐπὶ τῶν ἀδηφαγούντων.
ὅταν μὲν γὰρ ἀναδίδοταί τι τῶν καταποθέντων, ἑτοιμότερον ἡ γαστὴρ πέττει τὰ κατάλοιπα.
διαμένοντος δὲ ἐν αὐτῇ τοῦ πλήθους τῶν σιτίων, ὅταν ποτὲ βαρύνηται πρὸς αὐτῶν, ἀποτρίβεται πάντα πρὶν πεφθῆναι.
english_sentences: When, then, even though he has added the reasoning in reliance on which he advised [215] what he advised, some difficulty nevertheless remains, what must one suppose happens in those passages of his text in which he did not add the cause of the things he bids us do?

For my part, had he not added the words about those of dense flesh, I would admit that I was entirely at a loss, as in many other cases in which, though the author has added nothing of the sort, the exegetes with the greatest boldness declare whatever comes into their heads.
But since he himself made mention of those of dense flesh, he has given an occasion for us too to write something useful concerning such natures.

For these people very quickly accumulate a plethora, since they transpire deficiently; and because the distribution is for this reason held back in them, their excretions are in every case fluid, and sometimes not only fluid but also thin, especially in those who eat voraciously.

For when some part of what has been swallowed is distributed, the stomach concocts what remains more readily; but when the mass of food stays on in it, then, whenever it is weighed down by it, it throws everything off before it has been concocted.

beads.greek: ἴσως δὲ καὶ διὰ τὴν σκληρότητα τῶν φλεβῶν ἡ τῆς τροφῆς ἀνάδοσις ἐκωλύετο, [216] μὴ δυναμένων αὐτῶν ἐπὶ πλέον διαστείλασθαι, ἀλλὰ τήν γε τῶν τοιούτων φύσεων ἐπιμέλειαν ἐχρῆν αὐτὸν γεγραφέναι διὰ τῆς εἰς τοὐναντίον ἀγωγῆς.
beads.english: Perhaps the distribution of the nourishment was also hindered because of the hardness of the veins, [216] since they are unable to dilate any further.

beads.greek: ἀραίωσίς τε γὰρ καὶ μά- λαξις ὅλης τῆς ἕξεως εἰσὶν οἱ σκοποὶ, διὰ μαλακῆς τρίψεως καὶ λίπους πολλοῦ ἐν ταῖς πυέλοις γινόμεναι.
beads.english: But he ought at least to have written out the care of such natures by means of the course of treatment that leads towards the opposite.

beads.greek: ὁ δέ γε πρὸς τὸ σύμπτωμα μόνον ἵσταται, παραλιπὼν αὐτοῦ τὴν οἷον ῥί- ζαν ἐκκόψαι.
beads.english: For the aims are rarefaction and softening of the whole habit of body, brought about by gentle rubbing and plenty of oil in the bathing-tubs.

beads.greek: λέλεκται δὲ κατὰ τὴν προκειμένην ῥῆσιν καὶ τοῦτο αὐτῷ.
beads.english: He, however, takes his stand against the symptom alone, omitting to cut out what is, as it were, its root.

beads.greek: δῆλον γὰρ ὅτι ἡ κοιλία συνθάλπειν οὐ δύνα- ται. καὶ μὴν εἴπερ ἀληθῶς ᾐτιάσατο τὴν πυκνότητα τῆς ἕξεως καὶ τὰς φλέβας οὐκ ἀντιλαμβανομένας τῆς τροφῆς, οὐκ ὀρθῶς αἰτιᾶται τὴν κοιλίαν.
beads.english: And this too has been said by him in the passage before us: 'for it is clear that the belly cannot warm [the food] together.' And yet, if he truly blamed the density of the habit of body and the veins that do not take hold of the nourishment, he does not rightly blame the belly.

beads.greek: εἰ μέν τις αὐτῷ συγχω- ρήσειεν ἀληθεύειν ἐν τούτῳ, συγχωρήσειε καὶ τὴν ἐφεξῆς γεγραμμένην δίαιταν ὀρθῶς εἰρῆσθαι, τὸν ἔξοπτον ἄρτον καὶ τὸ ποτὸν εὔκρατον. ἔλαττον δὲ καὶ τὴν μονοσιτίαν καὶ τὸ μὴ περιπατεῖν ἐπὶ τοῖς σιτίοις.
beads.english: If one should grant him that he speaks the truth in this, one would also grant that the regimen written next is rightly stated: the thoroughly baked bread and the well-tempered drink; but less so both the taking of a single meal a day and the not walking after food.

greek_sentences: ἴσως δὲ καὶ διὰ τὴν σκληρότητα τῶν φλεβῶν ἡ τῆς τροφῆς ἀνάδοσις ἐκωλύετο, [216] μὴ δυναμένων αὐτῶν ἐπὶ πλέον διαστείλασθαι, ἀλλὰ τήν γε τῶν τοιούτων φύσεων ἐπιμέλειαν ἐχρῆν αὐτὸν γεγραφέναι διὰ τῆς εἰς τοὐναντίον ἀγωγῆς.
ἀραίωσίς τε γὰρ καὶ μά- λαξις ὅλης τῆς ἕξεως εἰσὶν οἱ σκοποὶ, διὰ μαλακῆς τρίψεως καὶ λίπους πολλοῦ ἐν ταῖς πυέλοις γινόμεναι.
ὁ δέ γε πρὸς τὸ σύμπτωμα μόνον ἵσταται, παραλιπὼν αὐτοῦ τὴν οἷον ῥί- ζαν ἐκκόψαι.
λέλεκται δὲ κατὰ τὴν προκειμένην ῥῆσιν καὶ τοῦτο αὐτῷ.
δῆλον γὰρ ὅτι ἡ κοιλία συνθάλπειν οὐ δύνα- ται.
καὶ μὴν εἴπερ ἀληθῶς ᾐτιάσατο τὴν πυκνότητα τῆς ἕξεως καὶ τὰς φλέβας οὐκ ἀντιλαμβανομένας τῆς τροφῆς, οὐκ ὀρθῶς αἰτιᾶται τὴν κοιλίαν.
εἰ μέν τις αὐτῷ συγχω- ρήσειεν ἀληθεύειν ἐν τούτῳ, συγχωρήσειε καὶ τὴν ἐφεξῆς γεγραμμένην δίαιταν ὀρθῶς εἰρῆσθαι, τὸν ἔξοπτον ἄρτον καὶ τὸ ποτὸν εὔκρατον.
ἔλαττον δὲ καὶ τὴν μονοσιτίαν καὶ τὸ μὴ περιπατεῖν ἐπὶ τοῖς σιτίοις.
english_sentences: Perhaps the distribution of the nourishment was also hindered because of the hardness of the veins, [216] since they are unable to dilate any further.
But he ought at least to have written out the care of such natures by means of the course of treatment that leads towards the opposite.
For the aims are rarefaction and softening of the whole habit of body, brought about by gentle rubbing and plenty of oil in the bathing-tubs.
He, however, takes his stand against the symptom alone, omitting to cut out what is, as it were, its root.

And this too has been said by him in the passage before us: 'for it is clear that the belly cannot warm [the food] together.' And yet, if he truly blamed the density of the habit of body and the veins that do not take hold of the nourishment, he does not rightly blame the belly.

If one should grant him that he speaks the truth in this, one would also grant that the regimen written next is rightly stated: the thoroughly baked bread and the well-tempered drink; but less so both the taking of a single meal a day and the not walking after food.

beads.greek: Ἐστὶ δὲ αὕτη μὲν ὀξείη ἡ φύσις καὶ τρέπεται ἐφ᾿ ἑκάτερα [217] καὶ ἀκμάζει ὀλίγον χρόνον ἡ εὐεξίη ἐν τοῖσι τοιουτοτρό- ποισι τῶν σωμάτων. Ὀξεῖαν εἶπε τὴν τῶν πυκνοσάρκων φύσιν, ἐν ἴσῳ τῷ ταχείας ποιουμένην τὰς μεταβολάς.
beads.english: "This nature is acute, and it turns to either side, [217] and good condition is at its peak only for a short time in bodies of this sort." He called the nature of those with dense flesh "acute", as equivalent to one that undergoes its changes quickly.

beads.greek: ἐπιφέρων γοῦν ἐρεῖ καὶ τρέπεται ἐφ᾿ ἑκάτερα, τουτέστιν ἐπί τε τὴν εὐεξίην καὶ τοὐναντίον.
beads.english: Accordingly, continuing, he will say "and it turns to either side", that is, both towards good condition and towards the opposite.

beads.greek: ἐφεξῆς δ᾿ ἔτι φησὶ, καὶ ἀκμάζει ὀλίγον χρόνον ἡ εὐεξίη ἐν τοῖσι τοιουτοτρόποισι τῶν σωμάτων. ἐδείχθη γὰρ ἐν τοῖς εἰς τοὺς ἀφορισμοὺς ὑπομνήμασιν ὅτι ἡ τῶν γυμναστικῶν εὐεξία μετὰ πληρώσεως αἵματός τε καὶ σαρκῶν τὴν ῥώμην φυλάττουσα τῶν φυσικῶν δυνάμεων.
beads.english: And next he says further: "and good condition is at its peak only for a short time in bodies of this sort." For it was shown in the commentaries on the Aphorisms that the good condition of athletes [is] with a filling of blood and flesh, preserving the strength of the natural faculties.

beads.greek: ἀλλ᾿ ὥσπερ ἐκεῖ τὴν ἐπ᾿ ἄκρον εὐεξίαν ἐδείκνυμεν εἶναι σφαλερὰν, οὐ ταχέως γιγνομένην ἐν τοῖς ἀραιοῖς σώμασιν, οὕτω καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν πυκνοσάρκων, ἐπεὶ τάχιστα γίνεται, διὰ τὸ δυσφόρητον ἀναγκαζομένη δηλονότι μεταπίπτειν εὐθέως ὀξεῖαν ποιεῖται τὴν γένεσιν καὶ τὴν λύσιν.
beads.english: But just as there we showed that good condition at its extreme is dangerous, though it does not come about quickly in loose-textured bodies, so also in those with dense flesh: since it comes about very quickly, and is of course compelled to change over at once because it is hard to bear, it makes both its coming-into-being and its dissolution acute.

greek_sentences: Ἐστὶ δὲ αὕτη μὲν ὀξείη ἡ φύσις καὶ τρέπεται ἐφ᾿ ἑκάτερα [217] καὶ ἀκμάζει ὀλίγον χρόνον ἡ εὐεξίη ἐν τοῖσι τοιουτοτρό- ποισι τῶν σωμάτων.
Ὀξεῖαν εἶπε τὴν τῶν πυκνοσάρκων φύσιν, ἐν ἴσῳ τῷ ταχείας ποιουμένην τὰς μεταβολάς.
ἐπιφέρων γοῦν ἐρεῖ καὶ τρέπεται ἐφ᾿ ἑκάτερα, τουτέστιν ἐπί τε τὴν εὐεξίην καὶ τοὐναντίον.
ἐφεξῆς δ᾿ ἔτι φησὶ, καὶ ἀκμάζει ὀλίγον χρόνον ἡ εὐεξίη ἐν τοῖσι τοιουτοτρόποισι τῶν σωμάτων.
ἐδείχθη γὰρ ἐν τοῖς εἰς τοὺς ἀφορισμοὺς ὑπομνήμασιν ὅτι ἡ τῶν γυμναστικῶν εὐεξία μετὰ πληρώσεως αἵματός τε καὶ σαρκῶν τὴν ῥώμην φυλάττουσα τῶν φυσικῶν δυνάμεων.

ἀλλ᾿ ὥσπερ ἐκεῖ τὴν ἐπ᾿ ἄκρον εὐεξίαν ἐδείκνυμεν εἶναι σφαλερὰν, οὐ ταχέως γιγνομένην ἐν τοῖς ἀραιοῖς σώμασιν, οὕτω καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν πυκνοσάρκων, ἐπεὶ τάχιστα γίνεται, διὰ τὸ δυσφόρητον ἀναγκαζομένη δηλονότι μεταπίπτειν εὐθέως ὀξεῖαν ποιεῖται τὴν γένεσιν καὶ τὴν λύσιν.
english_sentences: "This nature is acute, and it turns to either side, [217] and good condition is at its peak only for a short time in bodies of this sort." He called the nature of those with dense flesh "acute", as equivalent to one that undergoes its changes quickly.
Accordingly, continuing, he will say "and it turns to either side", that is, both towards good condition and towards the opposite.

And next he says further: "and good condition is at its peak only for a short time in bodies of this sort." For it was shown in the commentaries on the Aphorisms that the good condition of athletes [is] with a filling of blood and flesh, preserving the strength of the natural faculties.

But just as there we showed that good condition at its extreme is dangerous, though it does not come about quickly in loose-textured bodies, so also in those with dense flesh: since it comes about very quickly, and is of course compelled to change over at once because it is hard to bear, it makes both its coming-into-being and its dissolution acute.

beads.greek: [218] Τὰ δὲ ἀραιότερα τῶν εἰδέων καὶ δασύτερα καὶ τὴν κρεη- φαγίην δέχεται καὶ τὰς ταλαιπωρίας μᾶλλον ὑπομένει καὶ χρονιώτεραι γίνονται αὐτέοισιν αἱ εὐεξίαι.
beads.english: [218] But the looser-textured and hairier of the types both accept meat-eating and endure hardships better, and their good conditions become longer-lasting.

beads.greek: Ὅτι τὰ δασύτερα τῶν σωμάτων ἀραιότερον ἔχει τό τε δέρμα καὶ τὸ σαρκῶδες γένος ἐμάθομεν ἐν τοῖς περὶ κρά- σεων.
beads.english: That the hairier of bodies have both the skin and the fleshy kind of tissue looser in texture we learned in the books On Mixtures.

beads.greek: ταῦτ᾿ οὖν εἰκότως φησὶ καὶ τὴν κρεηφαγίαν ἀνέχε- σθαι μᾶλλον, ὡς ἂν διαπνεόμενα καὶ τὰς ταλαιπωρίας· ἧς- σον γὰρ ἁλίσκεται κόποις.
beads.english: These, then, he reasonably says tolerate meat-eating better, inasmuch as they are transpired through, and also hardships; for they are less overtaken by fatigues.

beads.greek: ἐμάθομεν καὶ τοῦτο ἐν τοῖς ὑγιεινοῖς.
beads.english: This too we learned in the books On Hygiene.

beads.greek: εἰ δὲ ταῦτα καὶ τὰς εὐεξίας ἕξει χρονιωτέρας, ὡς ἂν μὴ εἰς ἄκρον ἀφικνουμένας ἑτοίμως.
beads.english: And if these things are so (εἰ δὲ ταῦτα, text possibly corrupt), they will also have their good conditions longer-lasting, inasmuch as these do not readily reach the extreme.

greek_sentences: [218] Τὰ δὲ ἀραιότερα τῶν εἰδέων καὶ δασύτερα καὶ τὴν κρεη- φαγίην δέχεται καὶ τὰς ταλαιπωρίας μᾶλλον ὑπομένει καὶ χρονιώτεραι γίνονται αὐτέοισιν αἱ εὐεξίαι.
Ὅτι τὰ δασύτερα τῶν σωμάτων ἀραιότερον ἔχει τό τε δέρμα καὶ τὸ σαρκῶδες γένος ἐμάθομεν ἐν τοῖς περὶ κρά- σεων.
ταῦτ᾿ οὖν εἰκότως φησὶ καὶ τὴν κρεηφαγίαν ἀνέχε- σθαι μᾶλλον, ὡς ἂν διαπνεόμενα καὶ τὰς ταλαιπωρίας· ἧς- σον γὰρ ἁλίσκεται κόποις.
ἐμάθομεν καὶ τοῦτο ἐν τοῖς ὑγιεινοῖς.
εἰ δὲ ταῦτα καὶ τὰς εὐεξίας ἕξει χρονιωτέρας, ὡς ἂν μὴ εἰς ἄκρον ἀφικνουμένας ἑτοίμως.
english_sentences: [218] But the looser-textured and hairier of the types both accept meat-eating and endure hardships better, and their good conditions become longer-lasting.
That the hairier of bodies have both the skin and the fleshy kind of tissue looser in texture we learned in the books On Mixtures.
These, then, he reasonably says tolerate meat-eating better, inasmuch as they are transpired through, and also hardships; for they are less overtaken by fatigues.
This too we learned in the books On Hygiene.
And if these things are so (εἰ δὲ ταῦτα, text possibly corrupt), they will also have their good conditions longer-lasting, inasmuch as these do not readily reach the extreme.

beads.greek: Καὶ ὁκόσοι τὰ σιτία ἀνερεύγονται τῇ ὑστερέῃ καὶ τὰ ὑποχόνδρια μετεωρίζεται αὐτέοισιν, ὡς ἀπέπτων τῶν σιτίων ἐόντων, τουτέοισι καθεύδειν μὲν πλείονα χρόνον [219] ξυμφέρει, τῇ δὲ ἄλλῃ ταλαιπωρίῃ ἀναγκάζειν χρὴ αὐτῶν τὰ σώματα καὶ τὸν οἶνον ἀκρητέστερον πινόντων καὶ πλείω καὶ τοῖσι σιτίοισιν ἐλάσσοσι χρέεσθαι ὑπὸ τοῦτον τὸν χρό- νον. δῆλον γὰρ δὴ ὅτι ὑπ᾿ ἀσθενείης καὶ ψυχρότητος ἡ κοιλίη οὐ δύναται τὸ πλῆθος τῶν σιτίων καταπέσσειν.
beads.english: "And those who belch up their food on the following day, and whose hypochondria become distended, as though the food were undigested — for these it is beneficial to sleep for a longer time, [219] but in other respects one must force their bodies with exertion, and they should drink their wine less diluted and in greater quantity, and use less food during this time.

beads.greek: Καλῶς ἐποίησεν ἐνταῦθα προσθεὶς αὐτὸς ἐπὶ τῷ τέ- λει. δῆλον γὰρ δὴ ὅτι ὑπὸ ἀσθενείης καὶ ψυχρότητος ἡ κοιλία οὐ δύναται τὸ πλῆθος τῶν σιτίων καταπέσσειν.
beads.english: For it is plain that, through weakness and coldness, the belly is unable to concoct the quantity of the food." He did well here to add, himself, at the end: "For it is plain that, through weakness and coldness, the belly is unable to concoct the quantity of the food." For it is as looking to this aim that he tries to heat it thoroughly.

beads.greek: ὡς πρὸς τοῦτον γὰρ ἀποβλέπων τὸν σκοπὸν, ἐκθερμαίνειν αὐ- τὴν πειρᾶται. καὶ κατὰ τοῦτο καθεύδειν τε πλείω χρόνον αὐτοῖς συμβουλεύει καὶ γυμνάζεσθαι, καὶ τὸν οἶνον ἀκρα- τέστερον πίνειν καὶ πλείονα καὶ τοῖς σιτίοις ἐλάττοσι χρῆ- σθαι κατ᾿ ἐκεῖνον τὸν χρόνον, καθ᾿ ὃν ἂν ἠπεπτηκότες τυγ- χάνωσιν, ὡς ἄν γε τῷ λοιπῷ γυμναζόμενοί τε καὶ κινού- μενοι καὶ πίνοντες τὸν οἶνον, ὡς εἰρήκαμεν, οὐδέν τι δέον- ται τῆς συμμέτρου ποσότητος τῶν σιτίων ἀφαιρεῖν.
beads.english: And on this account he advises them both to sleep for a longer time and to exercise, and to drink their wine less diluted and in greater quantity, and to use less food at that time at which they happen to have failed to digest, since for the rest of the time, exercising and moving about and drinking the wine as we have said, they have no need at all to take anything away from the proportionate quantity of food.

beads.greek: [220] Ὁκόσους δὲ δίψαι λαμβάνουσιν, τουτέοισι τῶν τε σι- τίων καὶ τῶν ταλαιπωριῶν ἀφαιρέειν καὶ τὸν οἶνον πι- νόντων ὑδαρέα τε καὶ ὡς ὅτι ψυχρότατον. Νῦν μὲν οὕτως εἴρηται τὸ γνώρισμα τῶν θερμῶν φύ- σεων, ἐν δὲ τῷ ἕκτῳ τῶν ἐπιδημιῶν κατὰ τήνδε τὴν ῥῆ- σιν· ἐν θερμῷ φύσει ψυχρὸν ποτὸν ὕδωρ, ἐλινύειν.
beads.english: [220] "Those who are seized by thirsts: for these one should take away from both their foods and their exertions, and they should drink their wine watery and as cold as possible." Here the distinguishing sign of hot natures has been stated in this way, but in the sixth book of the Epidemics it is stated in the following passage: "In a hot nature, cold water as drink; to keep still." For he himself, having named the krasis of the body, wrote next the regimen which those so disposed require, a regimen having cooling as its principal point.

beads.greek: αὐ- τὸς γὰρ ὀνομάσας τὴν κρᾶσιν τοῦ σώματος ἐφεξῆς ἔγραψε τὴν δίαιταν ἦς χρῄζουσιν οἱ οὕτω διακείμενοι, κεφάλαιον μὲν ἔχουσαν τὴν ψύξιν. ἐν δὲ τῷ κεφαλαίῳ τούτῳ τῆς διαίτης τὰ δραστικώτερα, ἥ τε ὑδροποσία ἐστὶν καὶ ἡ ἀγυ- μνασία.
beads.english: And within this principal point of the regimen the more efficacious measures are water-drinking and abstention from exercise.

beads.greek: κατὰ δὲ τὴν προκειμένην ῥῆσιν τὸ μὲν ἐλινύειν ἕτερον ὠνόμασεν, εἰπὼν καὶ τῶν ταλαιπωριῶν ἀφαιρέειν. ἀντὶ δὲ τοῦ πίνειν ὕδωρ γράψας καὶ τὸν οἶνον πινόντων ὑδαρέα τε καὶ ὡς ὅτι ψυχρότατον καὶ μοι δοκεῖ κάλλιον ἐνταῦθα παραινέσαι.
beads.english: In the present passage, however, he named the "keeping still" differently, saying "and to take away from the exertions." And instead of "to drink water" he wrote "and they should drink their wine watery and as cold as possible"; and he seems to me to have given better advice here.

beads.greek: τὸ γὰρ ὑδαρὲς πόμα καὶ ψυχρὸν οὐκ ἐστέρηται μὲν τοῦ ἐμψύχειν, προσείληφε δὲ καὶ τὰς ἐκ τοῦ οἴνου ὠφελείας.
beads.english: For the watery and cold drink is not deprived of its cooling power, but it has also taken on the benefits that come from the wine.

beads.greek: [221] Ὁκόσοισι δὲ ὀδύναι γίγνονται ἐκ τῶν σπλάγχνων ἢ ἐκ γυ- μνασίης ἢ ἐξ ἄλλης τινὸς ὁδοιπορίης, τουτέοισι ξυμφέρει ἀναπαύεσθαι ἀσίτοισι.
beads.english: [221] Those who suffer pains from the viscera, or from exercise, or from some other journey, are benefited by resting without food.

beads.greek: πόματι δὲ χρέεσθαι ὅ τι ἐλάχι- στον εἰς τὸ σῶμα ἐσελθὸν, πλεῖστον οὖρον διάξει, ὅπως αἱ φλέβες, αἱ διὰ τῶν σπλάγχνων πεφυκυῖαι, μὴ κατατείνων- ται πληρώμεναι.
beads.english: And they should use a drink which, entering the body in the smallest quantity, will carry through the greatest amount of urine, so that the veins that grow through the viscera may not be stretched by being filled.

beads.greek: ἐκ γὰρ τῶν τοιουτέων τὰ φύματα γί- νονται καὶ οἱ πυρετοί.
beads.english: For from such things the growths and the fevers arise.

beads.greek: Περὶ πασῶν δὲ τῶν ὑποθηκῶν ἐν τῇ τῶν ὑγιεινῶν πραγματείᾳ τελέως διελήλυθα καὶ νῦν ὅσον ὑπομνήσεως ἕνεκα καθάπερ ἐν τοῖς ἔμπροσθεν, οὕτως καὶ κατὰ τήνδε τὴν ῥῆσιν εἰρήσεται.
beads.english: I have gone through all these precepts completely in the treatise on matters of health, and now, as in the preceding passages, so also in the case of this lemma, as much will be said as serves for a reminder.

beads.greek: πολλοῖς γὰρ τῶν ἀπυρέτων ὀδύναι ἐπιγίνονται κατὰ τὰ σπλάγχνα καὶ μάλιστα κατὰ τὸ ἧπαρ. ὅταν ἐπὶ σιτίοις γυμνασάμενοι τύχωσιν ἢ λουσάμενοι, καὶ γίνεται τοῦτο διὰ στενοχωρίαν μὲν τῶν ἐν τῷ σπλάγχνῳ διεξόδων πάχος τε τῶν ἀναφερομένων χυμῶν.
beads.english: For many people who are without fever are affected by pains in the viscera, and especially in the liver, when they happen to have exercised or bathed after food; and this comes about through the narrowness of the passages in the viscus and the thickness of the humours being conveyed upward.

english_sentences: [221] Those who suffer pains from the viscera, or from exercise, or from some other journey, are benefited by resting without food.

And they should use a drink which, entering the body in the smallest quantity, will carry through the greatest amount of urine, so that the veins that grow through the viscera may not be stretched by being filled.
For from such things the growths and the fevers arise.

I have gone through all these precepts completely in the treatise on matters of health, and now, as in the preceding passages, so also in the case of this lemma, as much will be said as serves for a reminder.

For many people who are without fever are affected by pains in the viscera, and especially in the liver, when they happen to have exercised or bathed after food; and this comes about through the narrowness of the passages in the viscus and the thickness of the humours being conveyed upward.

beads.greek: ἐμφραττόμε- νοι γὰρ καὶ ἐνισχόμενοι τοῖς στενοῖς πέρασι τῶν φλεβῶν, [222] καθ᾿ ἃ ἡ μετάληψις γίνεται τοῦ αἵματος ἐκ τῶν σιμῶν τοῦ ἥπατος εἰς τὰ κυρτὰ, κωλύουσι μὲν τὰς διεξόδους, διατεί- νουσι δὲ δηλονότι τὰς κατὰ τὰ σιμὰ τοῦ ἥπατος φλέβας, ἐφ᾿ αἷς οὕτω πασχούσαις ὀδυνῶνται χωρὶς τοῦ πυρέσσειν.
beads.english: For, being obstructed and held fast in the narrow ends of the veins, [222] at which the transfer of the blood takes place from the concave parts of the liver into the convex parts, they hinder the passages and, evidently, distend the veins in the concave parts of the liver; and when these are affected in this way, the patients feel pain without being feverish.

beads.greek: ἀναπαύεσθαι δὲ τούτους χρὴ καθ᾿ ὃν ἂν ἀλγῶσι χρόνον καὶ πίνειν τι τῶν οὐρητικῶν καὶ τὸ ἧπαρ ἐκφραττόντων.
beads.english: These people must rest for as long as they are in pain, and drink something from among the things that are diuretic and that clear obstructions from the liver.

beads.greek: ἂν γὰρ μὴ οὐρήσωσι, φύματα καὶ πυρετοὶ ταῖς τοιαύταις προ- φάσεσιν ἐπιγίνονται.
beads.english: For if they do not pass urine, growths and fevers supervene from such causes.

beads.greek: Ὁκόσοισι δὲ αἱ νοῦσοι ἀπὸ τοῦ ἐγκεφάλου γίνονται, νάρκη πρῶτον ἴσχει τὴν κεφαλὴν καὶ οὐρέει θαμινὰ καὶ τἄλλα πάσχει ὁκόσα περ ἐπὶ στραγγουρίῃ, οὗτος ἐφ᾿ ἡμέρας ἐννέα τοῦτο πάσχει.
beads.english: In those in whom the diseases arise from the brain, numbness first seizes the head, and he urinates frequently and suffers all the other things that occur in strangury; this man suffers this for nine days.

beads.greek: καὶ ἢν μὲν ῥαγῇ κατὰ τὰς ῥῖνας ἢ κατὰ τὰ ὦτα ὕδωρ ἢ βλέννα, ἀπαλλάσσεται τῆς νούσου καὶ τῆς στραγγουρίης παύεται.

english_sentences: For, being obstructed and held fast in the narrow ends of the veins, [222] at which the transfer of the blood takes place from the concave parts of the liver into the convex parts, they hinder the passages and, evidently, distend the veins in the concave parts of the liver; and when these are affected in this way, the patients feel pain without being feverish.
These people must rest for as long as they are in pain, and drink something from among the things that are diuretic and that clear obstructions from the liver.
For if they do not pass urine, growths and fevers supervene from such causes.

In those in whom the diseases arise from the brain, numbness first seizes the head, and he urinates frequently and suffers all the other things that occur in strangury; this man suffers this for nine days.
And if water or mucus breaks out through the nostrils or through the ears, he is released from the disease and ceases from the strangury.
He urinates painlessly, copiously and white, until twenty days have passed, and the pain leaves the man's head; but as he looks, the light of his eyes is stolen from him.

beads.greek: ἄνδρα δὲ χρὴ, ὅς ἐστι συνετὸς, [223] συλλογισάμενον, ὅτι τοῖσιν ἀνθρώποισι πλείστου ἄξιόν ἐστιν ἡ ὑγιείη, ἐπίστασθαι ἐκ τῆς ἑωϋτοῦ γνώμης ἐν τῇσι νούσοισιν ὠφελέεσθαι.
beads.english: "A man who is intelligent, [223] having reckoned that health is of the greatest worth to human beings, ought to know how to be helped in diseases by his own judgement." With good reason people have suspected this passage, and some have even condemned it outright, as written neither by Polybus nor, still less, by Hippocrates.

beads.greek: Εἰκότως ὑπωπτεύκασι ταύτην τὴν ῥῆσιν ἔνιοι δὲ καὶ τελείως κατεγνώκασιν, ὡς οὔτε Πολύβου γεγραφότος αὐτὴν οὔτε πολὺ μᾶλλον Ἱπποκράτους.
beads.english: For the beginning of the account is altogether lacking in distinction, claiming that the diseases arising from the brain bring on numbness and strangury.

beads.greek: ἥ τε γὰρ ἀρχὴ τοῦ λόγου παντάπασιν ἀδιόριστος, ἀξιοῦσα τὰς ἀπὸ τοῦ ἐγκεφάλου νάρκην τε καὶ στραγγουρίαν ἐπιφέρειν οὔτε εἴπερ ἡγήσαιτό τις αὐτὸν οὐ πάσας τὰς ἀπὸ τοῦ ἐγκεφάλου νόσους ἀποφαί- νεσθαι τοιαύτας ὑπάρχειν, ἀλλὰ μόνας ἐφ᾿ ὧν κατὰ τὰ ὦτα καὶ τὰς ῥῖνας ὕδωρ καὶ βλέννα ῥυεῖσα τὴν νόσον ἔπαυ- σεν, ἀληθὲς τὸ λεγόμενον, οὔτε γὰρ ἀεὶ φαίνεται τοῦτο γι- γνόμενον οὔθ᾿ ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολύ.
beads.english: Nor is what is said true even if one were to suppose that he declares not all the diseases arising from the brain to be of this kind, but only those in which water and mucus flowing out through the ears and the nostrils have put an end to the disease. For this is not seen to happen always, nor even for the most part.

greek_sentences: ἄνδρα δὲ χρὴ, ὅς ἐστι συνετὸς, [223] συλλογισάμενον, ὅτι τοῖσιν ἀνθρώποισι πλείστου ἄξιόν ἐστιν ἡ ὑγιείη, ἐπίστασθαι ἐκ τῆς ἑωϋτοῦ γνώμης ἐν τῇσι νούσοισιν ὠφελέεσθαι.
Εἰκότως ὑπωπτεύκασι ταύτην τὴν ῥῆσιν ἔνιοι δὲ καὶ τελείως κατεγνώκασιν, ὡς οὔτε Πολύβου γεγραφότος αὐτὴν οὔτε πολὺ μᾶλλον Ἱπποκράτους.

ἥ τε γὰρ ἀρχὴ τοῦ λόγου παντάπασιν ἀδιόριστος, ἀξιοῦσα τὰς ἀπὸ τοῦ ἐγκεφάλου νάρκην τε καὶ στραγγουρίαν ἐπιφέρειν οὔτε εἴπερ ἡγήσαιτό τις αὐτὸν οὐ πάσας τὰς ἀπὸ τοῦ ἐγκεφάλου νόσους ἀποφαί- νεσθαι τοιαύτας ὑπάρχειν, ἀλλὰ μόνας ἐφ᾿ ὧν κατὰ τὰ ὦτα καὶ τὰς ῥῖνας ὕδωρ καὶ βλέννα ῥυεῖσα τὴν νόσον ἔπαυ- σεν, ἀληθὲς τὸ λεγόμενον, οὔτε γὰρ ἀεὶ φαίνεται τοῦτο γι- γνόμενον οὔθ᾿ ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολύ.
english_sentences: "A man who is intelligent, [223] having reckoned that health is of the greatest worth to human beings, ought to know how to be helped in diseases by his own judgement." With good reason people have suspected this passage, and some have even condemned it outright, as written neither by Polybus nor, still less, by Hippocrates.
For the beginning of the account is altogether lacking in distinction, claiming that the diseases arising from the brain bring on numbness and strangury.

Nor is what is said true even if one were to suppose that he declares not all the diseases arising from the brain to be of this kind, but only those in which water and mucus flowing out through the ears and the nostrils have put an end to the disease.
For this is not seen to happen always, nor even for the most part.
